blocks.heading: CHAPTER 5 — What’s Wrong? Shū mālak? | شو مالك؟
paragraphs: Shū mālak? (or shū mālik for feminine) is one of the most common ways to check in on someone in Levantine Arabic. It goes beyond a simple “How are you?” and shows you actually care — asking what’s really going on when someone seems off, tired, upset, or not themselves.

This chapter focuses on emotional and physical states — how to describe how you’re feeling and what’s happening inside. You’ll learn vocabulary and patterns for emotions and conditions like I’m stressed, I’m really tired, I feel overwhelmed, I’m sad, and many more. Along the way, we’ll also cover family members and introduce the verbal noun (maṣdar) so you can talk more smoothly about activities.
You’ll also pick up a few small expressions that people use all the time: “it looks like…”, “really”, “kinda / sort of”, “what’s wrong?”, and “honestly.”

We’re covering emotional and physical states fairly early because this is some of the first language you’ll need to actually get your needs met. When you’re traveling or living in the Arab world, being able to clearly say how you feel can make a big difference — whether you’re connecting with people, asking for help, or explaining what’s going on.

This chapter builds directly on Chapters 3 and 4. Now that you can talk about possession and what you want, and connect ideas with conjunctions, we’re adding the ability to express how you are and how others are feeling. In real conversations, these ideas flow together naturally: “I want to go home because I’m exhausted,” “Honestly, I’m really stressed out right now,” or “It looks like he’s kinda sad. What’s wrong?”

blocks.heading: Important
blocks.text: Say everything out loud as you work through the chapter. Reading and filling in drills is not enough — speaking the words, sentences, and conversations aloud is one of the most important keys to making the language stick and sound natural.

blocks.heading: EVERYDAY EXPRESSION — I hope you feel better | سلامتك | salāmtak
paragraphs: سَلامْتَك (salāmtak) is one of the most common expressions you will hear when someone is sick, hurt, exhausted, or recovering from something. There is no single perfect English translation. Depending on the situation, it can mean “I hope you feel better,” “get well soon,” “glad you’re okay,” or simply “wishing you good health.”
Naturally, this expression changes depending on who you are speaking to:

You can use سَلامْتَك (salāmtak) after someone tells you they are sick, in pain, injured, or not feeling well. You can also say it when visiting someone who is recovering from an illness, accident, or surgery.

blocks.heading: Possessive Suffixes with Family Words
paragraphs: Because Arabic distinguishes between your father’s side and your mother’s side, family relationships are often much more precise than they are in English.
Adding the possessive suffix ـي changes these words to mean “my.”

blocks.heading: Feminine Spelling Change
paragraphs: When a feminine family word ends in ـة, the ة changes to ت before the possessive suffix is added.
This is the same spelling pattern you’ve already seen with other feminine nouns.

blocks.heading: Building Family Relationships with إضافة
paragraphs: Once you know the basic family words, you can combine them using الإضافة to describe more specific family relationships.
Notice what happened. You did not learn four completely new vocabulary words. You simply combined words you already know using الإضافة.

This pattern appears everywhere in Arabic family vocabulary, so do not try to memorize every possible relationship at once. Learn the core family words first. Once you know them, building the إضافة structure is usually simple: begin with the person you are describing, then add the family member who connects that person to you.
For example:

You will see this pattern again with grandchildren, in-laws, and many other family relationships. Once you understand the structure, you can build the expression instead of memorizing a separate word for every person.

In colloquial Arabic, you will also hear نَسيب (nasīb) for an in-law / relative by marriage, with the plural نَسايِب (nasāyib). Because نَسيب is a broader relationship term, speakers often still use the إضافة pattern when they want to specify exactly how someone is related.

items.explanation: ¹ Note: العيد (il-ʿīd) means “the holiday” or “the celebration.” In Jordan and Palestine, it usually refers to one of the two major Muslim holidays: عِيد الفِطْر (ʿĪd il-Fiṭr), celebrated at the end of Ramadan, or عِيد الأَضْحى (ʿĪd il-Aḍḥā), the Festival of Sacrifice. During Eid, families commonly gather, visit relatives, share meals, and celebrate together. The word عِيد can also refer to other religious holidays, such as Christmas or Easter. In everyday conversation, speakers often simply say العيد because everyone understands which holiday they mean from the context.

lessons.title: Expressing Emotional & Physical States — التعبير عن الحالات العاطفية والجسدية | it-taʿbīr ʿan il-ḥālāt il-ʿāṭifiyye w il-jasadiyye

paragraphs: In Levantine Arabic, many emotional and physical states are expressed using describing words that function much like adjectives.
You already know how to describe people and objects without using a present-tense form of “to be.” The same principle applies when describing how someone feels.

blocks.heading: Recognizing Common Patterns
paragraphs: These sentences follow a familiar pattern:
Person + describing word = a statement about someone’s condition or state.
There are two useful patterns to notice in this chapter.

blocks.heading: Pattern 1: Describing words beginning with مـ
paragraphs: Several common emotional and physical states begin with مـ.

These words do not all belong to the same grammatical category. Some are active participles, while others are passive participles. For now, you do not need to distinguish between them. You only need to recognize their meanings and learn how they change depending on the person being described. We'll explore their grammatical structures more deeply in Arabic After Verbs.

blocks.heading: Pattern 2: Describing words ending with ـان
paragraphs: Another common pattern includes describing words that end with ـان (-ān) in their masculine form.
Many of these words describe physical or emotional conditions.
Recognizing these patterns will make the vocabulary easier to remember, but do not assume every describing word follows one of these patterns.

blocks.heading: Main Idea
blocks.text: For now, treat these words as descriptions of someone’s emotional or physical state. Your goal is to learn their meanings, recognize their forms, and use them naturally in sentences without conjugating verbs.

blocks.heading: Agreement
paragraphs: Like the adjectives you've already learned, words describing emotional and physical states agree with the person being described.
In this chapter, we'll focus on three forms:
Masculine singular
Feminine singular
Plural for people
Many of these words form their plural with ـين (-īn), but that isn't true of every adjective. Learn each word's three forms together rather than assuming they all follow the same pattern.
Let's look at some examples.

Some sentences will include new vocabulary. That is okay. Take notes on any new words that help the sentence make sense. This gives you a two-for-one: you learn a new supporting word, and that word helps you remember the main vocabulary word more strongly.

paragraphs: You already know how prepositions connect nouns to locations and relationships:
Now, we will use these same prepositions with states of being.
In Arabic, some states feel complete on their own:

When you want to explain what caused a feeling or what it relates to, Arabic often pairs the describing word with a particular preposition. These natural pairings are called collocations—meaning certain words naturally go together.
For example, in English we say:
tired from work
ready for class
interested in Arabic
late for the appointment
Arabic works the same way, but the preposition is not always what you would expect from English. That is why it is best to learn these combinations as complete chunks.

blocks.heading: Here is how they appear in context:

items.en: We are late for the appointment

blocks.heading: Main idea
blocks.text: You are not learning a new grammar system. You are combining states of being with prepositions you already know. The key is recognizing which preposition naturally belongs with each state.

blocks.heading: Part A — Build the Correct Combination
paragraphs: Complete each sentence using the correct state of being and its accompanying preposition.

Pay attention to masculine, feminine, and plural agreement. Remember that بـ (b-) and لـ (l-) attach directly to the following word, while prepositions such as مِن (min), عَن (ʿan), and عَ (ʿa) are written separately.
For sentences beginning with “I,” the speaker's gender is indicated when needed.
Say each completed sentence out loud. Repetition is your friend.

blocks.heading: 5.4 “Honestly…” — بصراحة | bi-ṣarāḥa
paragraphs: In this chapter, you are learning how to describe states of being: tired, busy, comfortable, annoyed, happy, stressed, and so on.
In real conversation, sometimes you do not want to just say the state. You want to signal that you are being direct.
That is where بِصَراحة comes in handy.
The word بِصَراحة is built from two parts:
So the literal meaning is something like with honesty or in honesty. In natural English, we usually translate it as honestly or to be honest.

Arabic conversation often has a strong sense of politeness and social balance. So when you want to say something honestly, especially if it is a little negative, personal, or direct, بِصَراحة helps prepare the listener.
It is like saying:
Honestly…
To be honest…
Honestly, here’s how it is…

blocks.heading: Formula
blocks.text: بِصَراحة + complete sentence = Honestly / To be honest, ...

blocks.heading: Use بِصَراحة at the beginning of a sentence to introduce an honest opinion, feeling, or explanation.

items.en: Honestly, I'm comfortable in this place

blocks.heading: Main Idea
blocks.text: Use بِصَراحة when you want to sound honest, direct, or clear about how you feel. It is a small expression, but it makes your Arabic sound much more natural in real conversation.

blocks.heading: "What's Wrong?" — shū mālak? | شو مالك؟
paragraphs: When you are talking about how people feel, you also need a natural way to ask what is going on with someone.
In Jordanian and Palestinian Arabic, two very common questions are:

items.en: What’s with you? / What’s going on with you?

paragraphs: Both are used every day and are widely understood across Jordan and Palestine.
شُو مالَك؟ is usually the more neutral and caring expression. It can mean:
What’s wrong?
What’s the matter?
Are you okay?
Use it when someone seems tired, upset, sick, quiet, or not like themselves.

items.en: What’s wrong? Are you all tired?

blocks.heading: The ending changes depending on who you are talking to:
شُو فيك؟
paragraphs: شُو فيك؟ can also mean “What’s wrong?”, but it often feels more like:
What’s with you?
What’s going on with you?
Depending on tone, it can be neutral, concerned, or a little stronger, especially if you are reacting to someone’s behavior.

items.en: What’s going on with you? Are you tired?
What’s going on with you all? Are you upset?

blocks.heading: QUICK PRONUNCIATION NOTE — When Does the Feminine Ending Become -ki?
paragraphs: In Levantine Arabic, you’ve already learned that words change depending on whether you’re addressing a man or a woman.
But there’s an important pronunciation pattern worth recognizing.
When a long vowel comes directly before the final ك (-k) in the masculine form, the feminine form commonly adds an -i sound after the k.
Let’s look at three examples.
Notice the long ī immediately before the final k.
The masculine form ends in -k, while the feminine form ends in -ki.
Here, the long vowel is ē.
Again, the feminine form ends in -ki.

paragraphs: Here, the word before the pronoun suffix ends in a consonant rather than a long vowel.
The masculine and feminine forms differ through the short vowel before the k.
A useful pattern in everyday Levantine Arabic is that when a possessive or attached pronoun ending follows a long vowel, the masculine form often ends in -k and the feminine form in -ki.

After a consonant, common forms such as عِنْدَك / عِنْدِك (ʿindak / ʿindik) instead distinguish masculine and feminine through the vowel before the final k.
These are useful patterns for recognizing and producing everyday speech. The exact pronunciations and spellings can vary somewhat across speakers and regions.
For now, focus on recognizing the patterns in the expressions you've already learned.

blocks.text: Learn to recognize whether the pronoun suffix follows a long vowel or a consonant. This will help you pronounce unfamiliar forms more naturally, rather than memorizing every variation separately.

blocks.heading: Putting It All Together
paragraphs: Now let’s connect this with a very common way to answer. When someone asks شُو مالَك؟ or شُو فيك؟, you can answer with بِصَراحة (bi-ṣarāḥa), meaning “honestly” or “to be honest.” This is a natural pattern you will hear all the time when someone explains what is really going on.

blocks.heading: You can also use it with شُو فيك؟

items.en: What’s going on with you all?

blocks.heading: Understanding Activities as Nouns
paragraphs: Up to this point, you’ve learned how to talk about people, objects, places, feelings, and possession without conjugating verbs.
Now we’re going to introduce another important concept: the verbal noun, called المَصْدَر (il-maṣdar) in Arabic.
A verbal noun is a noun that names an action, activity, or event.
Think about the difference between these two English expressions:
I’m studying.
Studying is important.
In the first sentence, studying is part of a verb construction. It tells us what someone is doing.
In the second sentence, studying functions as a noun. We’re talking about the activity itself.
Arabic uses verbal nouns in much the same way.

blocks.heading: Rule 1 — A Verbal Noun Behaves Like a Regular Noun
paragraphs: Notice that these words name activities without telling us who is performing them or when they’re happening.
That’s what makes them useful.
Although verbal nouns are related to verbs, they function grammatically as nouns.
This means you can use them in many of the same sentence structures you’ve already learned.
For example:
These are all nominal sentences. You haven’t conjugated a single verb.
Notice something else: just like ordinary nouns, verbal nouns have grammatical gender.
الدِّراسة is feminine, so we use مُهِمّة.
التَّمْرين is masculine, so we use مُهِمّ.
The same adjective agreement rules you’ve already learned still apply.

blocks.heading: What About the Verbs?
paragraphs: Every verbal noun has a grammatical relationship to a verb, but we aren’t going to study how these forms are derived just yet.
We’ll explore that relationship in detail in Arabic After Verbs. For now, learn each verbal noun as an independent vocabulary word.

blocks.heading: WHAT TO REMEMBER
blocks.text: A verbal noun allows you to talk about an action or activity as a thing. Once you recognize it as a noun, you can begin using the grammar you already know to build more complete sentences. On the next page, we’ll see how verbal nouns work with the definite article الـ and possessive suffixes.

blocks.heading: What to Remember
blocks.text: Verbal nouns follow the same rules of definiteness as other nouns. Sometimes they appear with الـ, and sometimes they don’t. The sentence determines which form is appropriate.

paragraphs: Just like other nouns, verbal nouns can take possessive pronoun suffixes.

blocks.heading: Rule 4 — Verbal Nouns Can Form إضافة Constructions
paragraphs: Finally, here’s the last rule. You’ve already learned that إضافة (iḍāfa) connects two nouns to express a relationship between them.
For example:
Since verbal nouns behave like regular nouns, they can also form إضافة constructions.
This allows us to connect an activity directly to another noun.
Let’s look at some examples:

blocks.heading: Understanding the Relationship
paragraphs: Consider this example:
قِراية الكْتاب — reading the book
The first noun names the activity: reading.
The second noun identifies what is being read: the book.
Now consider:
سَواقة أَبوي — my dad’s driving
Here, the second noun identifies the person performing the activity.
Both expressions follow the same إضافة structure, even though the relationship between the nouns is different.

blocks.heading: Remember the إضافة Pattern
paragraphs: Just as with ordinary nouns, the first noun in an إضافة construction does not take the definite article الـ.
Compare:
Notice that القِراية no longer has الـ when it becomes the first noun in the إضافة construction.
The second noun helps determine whether the complete expression is definite.

blocks.heading: What to Remember
blocks.text: A verbal noun can connect directly to another noun through إضافة. The first noun names the activity, while the second identifies what that activity relates to.

blocks.heading: Usage in Real Life
paragraphs: Now that you understand how verbal nouns work, let’s look at how they appear in everyday conversation.
One of the most useful things about verbal nouns is that they allow you to talk about activities without conjugating verbs.
You can describe what someone is busy with, what they’re interested in, what they’re worried about, or what comes before or after something.
And the best part? You already know the grammar needed to build these sentences.

items.en: My daughter is afraid of driving
My brother is excited about traveling

paragraphs: Let’s start with some familiar situations.

You haven’t learned a new sentence structure. You’ve simply replaced an ordinary noun with a verbal noun.
Verbal nouns are also useful when discussing everyday routines, appointments, and schedules.
You already know expressions like بَعْد (after), قَبْل (before), and وَقْت (time).
Now look at what happens when we combine them with verbal nouns.

blocks.heading: 3. On Signs, Applications, and Public Notices
paragraphs: Notice that English sometimes translates a verbal noun using an -ing word, such as exercising or walking. Other times, it uses an ordinary noun, such as sleep or workout.
The important thing is the function of the Arabic word, not how English translates it.
You’ll also encounter verbal nouns throughout the Arab world on signs, websites, and phone applications.
These expressions often use more formal written Arabic than the colloquial language you’re learning, but the verbal nouns still function as nouns.
You don’t need to memorize every expression here. The goal is to recognize verbal nouns when you encounter them outside the classroom.

blocks.heading: WHAT TO REMEMBER
blocks.text: Verbal nouns aren’t limited to vocabulary lists or grammar exercises. They are useful in conversations about daily activities, feelings, schedules, and everyday experiences. Whether you’re describing an activity or reading about one on a sign, the verbal noun is still functioning as a noun. You've now seen how verbal nouns behave like ordinary nouns, take possessive suffixes, and form إضافة constructions. On the next page, we'll bring these ideas together and practice using them with the prepositions and states of being you already know.

blocks.heading: A Familiar Pattern
paragraphs: Remember the hidden t in feminine nouns ending in ة. It comes back when the word connects forward, whether to a possessive suffix or to the next noun in an إضافة.
The same pattern applies to verbal nouns.

paragraphs: This is the same pattern you learned with ordinary feminine nouns. You’re simply applying it to verbal nouns.
Now let’s combine verbal nouns with إضافة, prepositions, and states of being.

items.en: My sister is interested in reading the book

paragraphs: Here, قِراية الكْتاب forms an إضافة construction, while بِـ connects the entire expression to مِهْتَمّة.

items.en: My mom is busy cooking dinner

paragraphs: The verbal noun طَبْخ is connected directly to العَشا, telling us what is being cooked.

items.en: My dad is busy cleaning the house

paragraphs: Once again, تَنْضيف البَيْت identifies an activity, and بِـ connects it to the person’s state of being.

blocks.heading: Main Idea
blocks.text: Verbal nouns behave like regular nouns. They can take الـ, attach to possessive suffixes, and form إضافة constructions. They also work naturally with prepositions and states of being. Most importantly, you can use these structures to discuss everyday activities without conjugating verbs. blocks.heading: Talking About People’s States of Being
paragraphs: At this point, you already know how to form basic ideas without a verb in Arabic. You can say things like:
So far, you have been making direct descriptions. Now we are going to step it up and introduce a small construction that makes talking about people feel much smoother and more natural:
This construction is very common in everyday Palestinian and Jordanian Arabic. It lets you describe how someone seems based on appearance, mood, or first impression.

The word شَكْل means shape, look, or appearance. When we attach a possessive pronoun suffix, it gives the idea of “his look,” “her look,” or “its look.” In natural English, we usually translate it as looks or seems.

One important point is that the adjective must agree with the person or thing being described. If you use a feminine pronoun, the adjective must be feminine. If you use a plural pronoun, the adjective must be plural. Masculine nouns take masculine adjectives.

blocks.heading: Formula
blocks.text: The formula is: shikl + pronoun suffix + state / description

paragraphs: This is useful because it lets you talk about people without sounding too absolute. You are not always saying, “He is tired” as a fact. Instead, you are saying, “He looks tired” or “He seems tired.”
Compare:

The first sentence is direct. The second sentence is softer and more natural when you are judging from what you see. In everyday conversation, native speakers use شَكْل all the time when they are making observations about other people.
For now, treat شِكْلُه / شِكْلها / شِكْلهُم as an easy everyday tool for talking about someone’s state of being. Later, we will also use it with colors, body features, and more detailed descriptions.

lessons.title: Putting It All Together — Chapter 5 Conclusion

blocks.heading: Chapter 5 Conclusion — Putting It All Together
paragraphs: In this chapter, you learned how to talk about people’s emotional and physical states, especially through family vocabulary and everyday situations. You also learned how to describe activities using verbal nouns, and how to make your descriptions stronger or softer with كْتير and شْوَيّ.
Here are the main pieces we covered:

items.en: What’s with you? — to a woman
What’s with you? — to a man
a little / kind of, with adjectives

paragraphs: Before we move into the conversation, take a second to notice how much you can actually do now.

You are not just memorizing words anymore. You can talk about your family, describe how people feel, explain why someone wants something, and talk about everyday activities like studying, reading, driving, exercising, sleeping, and working.
That is real life Arabic.

If you travel to Jordan, Palestine, or anywhere in the Arab world, these are the kinds of things you will hear and use constantly. People talk about who is tired, who is busy, who is worried, who wants coffee, who has work, and who needs rest.

You are making big steps here. You are learning how to take small pieces — nouns, adjectives, possession, desire, prepositions, states of being, and verbal nouns — and connect them into speech that actually means something.
Now watch how these pieces work together in a short, natural conversation.

blocks.heading: Putting It All Together
paragraphs: Yousef and Walid are good friends who haven’t seen each other in a while. When they finally meet, Walid notices that Yousef looks tired and asks what’s been going on.
Yousef explains that he’s been balancing work and studying for the Tawjihi, making this one of the busiest times of the year for him.

As they continue talking, the conversation shifts to Yousef’s family. His mother is worried about his younger brother, who seems to be spending more time with his friends than studying. Yousef also talks about his sister, who successfully completed the Tawjihi last year and is now balancing a new job with preparations for university.

Like many everyday conversations, their discussion moves naturally from one topic to another. This gives you a chance to see how the grammar and vocabulary from this chapter come together in real-life Jordanian and Palestinian Arabic.

You may hear a few expressions you have not studied yet, such as أصعب من (aṣʿab min, “harder than”) and أصعب (“hardest” in context). These preview comparatives and superlatives, which you will learn in Volume Two. For now, focus on understanding the conversation; you do not need to produce these forms yet.

blocks.title: Yousef and Walid
blocks.context: Yousef and Walid are good friends who haven’t seen each other in a while. When they finally meet, Walid notices that Yousef looks tired and asks what’s been going on.

lines.speaker: Walid
lines.ar: مرحبا يا يوسف، شو مالك؟ شكلك تعبان كتير.
lines.translit: marḥaba yā Yūsuf, shū mālak? shiklak taʿbān ktīr.
lines.en: Hey Yousef, what’s wrong? You look really tired.

lines.speaker: Yousef
lines.ar: آه والله، أنا تعبان من الشّغل، ومشغول بالدّراسة كمان.
lines.translit: āh wallāh, ana taʿbān min ish-shughl, w-mashghūl bid-dirāse kamān.
lines.en: Yeah, I’m tired from work, and I’m busy with studying too.

lines.speaker: Walid
lines.ar: والدّراسة؟ صعبة هالأسبوع؟
lines.translit: w-id-dirāse? ṣaʿbe hal-usbūʿ?
lines.en: And studying? Is it difficult this week?

lines.speaker: Yousef
lines.ar: آه، صعبة شويّ، بسّ مهمّة عشان التّوجيهي.
lines.translit: āh, ṣaʿbe shwayy, bass muhimme ʿashān it-tawjīhī.
lines.en: Yeah, it’s a little difficult, but it’s important because of the Tawjihi.

lines.speaker: Walid
lines.ar: آه، هاي أصعب فترة بالسّنة.
lines.translit: āh, hāy aṣʿab fatra bis-sane.
lines.en: Yeah, this is the hardest time of the year.

lines.speaker: Yousef
lines.ar: صحيح. الدّرس كلّ أسبوع أصعب من اللّي قبله.
lines.translit: ṣaḥīḥ. id-dars kull usbūʿ aṣʿab min illī ʾablo.
lines.en: True. The lesson each week is harder than the one before it.

lines.speaker: Walid
lines.ar: وكيف إمّك؟
lines.translit: w-kīf immak?
lines.en: And how’s your mom?

lines.speaker: Yousef
lines.ar: إمّي قلقانة كتير ع أخوي الصغير.
lines.translit: immī ʾalʾāne ktīr ʿa akhūy iẓ-ẓghīr.
lines.en: My mom is really worried about my little brother.

lines.speaker: Walid
lines.ar: شو فيه؟
lines.translit: shū fīh?
lines.en: What’s with him?

lines.speaker: Yousef
lines.ar: شكله مشغول بالقعدة مع أصحابه أكتر من الدّراسة هالأيّام.
lines.translit: shiklo mashghūl bil-ʾaʿde maʿ aṣḥābo aktar min id-dirāse hal-ayyām.
lines.en: He seems to be spending more time hanging out with his friends than studying these days.

lines.speaker: Walid
lines.ar: عنجد؟ هاي مشكلة. وأختك؟
lines.translit: ʿanjad? hāy mushkile. w-ukhtak?
lines.en: Seriously? That’s a problem. And your sister?

lines.speaker: Yousef
lines.ar: أختي مسؤولة كتير. وعندها شغل جديد بالكافيه، وكمان عندها تسجيل بالجامعة بآخر السّنة.
lines.translit: ukhtī masʾūle ktīr. w-ʿindha shughl jdīd bil-kāfēh, w-kamān ʿindha tasjīl bil-jāmʿa bi-ākhir is-sane.
lines.en: My sister is really responsible. She has a new job at the café, and she also has university registration at the end of the year.

lines.speaker: Walid
lines.ar: ما شاء الله، شكلها جدّيّة كتير.
lines.translit: mā shāʾ Allāh, shiklha jiddiyye ktīr.
lines.en: Mashallah, she seems really serious.

lines.speaker: Yousef
lines.ar: معك حقّ، بسّ ما عندها وقت لحالها.
lines.translit: maʿak ḥaʾʾ, bass mā ʿindha waʾt laḥālha.
lines.en: You’re right, but she doesn’t have any time for herself.

lines.speaker: Walid
lines.ar: بسّ الرّاحة مهمّة كمان. مش كلّ إشي دراسة وامتحانات.
lines.translit: bass ir-rāḥa muhimme kamān. mish kull ishi dirāse w-imtiḥānāt.
lines.en: But rest is important too. Not everything is studying and exams.

lines.speaker: Yousef
lines.ar: آه، بسّ إحنا فخورين فيها كتير بنجاحها بالتّوجيهي السّنة الماضية.
lines.translit: āh, bass iḥna fakhūrīn fīha ktīr bi-najāḥha bit-tawjīhī is-sane il-māḍye.
lines.en: Yeah, but we’re really proud of her for passing the Tawjihi exam last year.

lines.speaker: Walid
lines.ar: طيّب، شو رأيك بلمّة عيلة بعد الامتحانات؟ شويّة راحة وتغيير جوّ.
lines.translit: ṭayyib, shū raʾyak bi-lammet ʿēle baʿd il-imtiḥānāt? shwayyet rāḥa w-taghyīr jaww.
lines.en: Well, how about a family get-together after the exams? A little rest and a change of scenery.

lines.speaker: Yousef
lines.ar: بصراحة، فكرة حلوة. كلّنا بدنا عطلة.
lines.translit: bi-ṣarāḥa, fikra ḥilwe. kullna bidna ʿuṭle.
lines.en: Honestly, that’s a nice idea. We all need a vacation.

lines.speaker: Walid
lines.ar: يا يوسف، الصّبر مفتاح الفرج. شويّ شويّ، وكلّ إشي رح يكون تمام.
lines.translit: yā Yūsuf, iṣ-ṣabr miftāḥ il-faraj. shwayy shwayy, w-kull ishi raḥ ykūn tamām.
lines.en: Yousef, patience is the key to relief. Little by little, everything will be fine.

lines.speaker: Yousef
lines.ar: والله معك حقّ. وبعد الامتحانات، العشا عليّ!
lines.translit: wallāh maʿak ḥaʾʾ. w-baʿd il-imtiḥānāt, il-ʿasha ʿalayy!
lines.en: You’re right. And after the exams, dinner’s on me!

paragraphs: Most of what you just read came from things you have already learned in this chapter. But there are a few parts of the conversation that are worth talking about because they tell you a little more about how people actually speak and about what is happening in the scene.
Early in the conversation, Yousef says:

items.ar: آه والله، أنا تعبان من الشغل، ومشغول بالدراسة كمان.
items.translit: āh wallāh, ana taʿbān min ish-shughl, w-mashghūl bid-dirāse kamān.
items.en: Yeah, I’m tired from work, and I’m busy with studying too.

paragraphs: You are going to hear آه والله a lot. Yousef is not making some dramatic oath here. In a conversation like this, it can just add a little emphasis to what he is saying—something like “yeah, seriously” or even just a stronger, more natural “yeah.”
You probably also noticed that the التوجيهي comes up more than once in this conversation, so let me give you a little background on the Tawjihi.

The Tawjihi is the major secondary-school exam students take at the end of high school in Jordan and Palestine. It is a big deal. A student’s result can have a major effect on their university options and what they are able to study afterward. Because of that, there can be a lot of pressure surrounding it—not just for the student, but for the whole family.

That gives you a little more context for what is happening in our scene. Yousef is studying for his Tawjihi now, so when he talks about being tired and busy with studying, there is a reason behind it. His sister has already been through the same experience, and she did well.
Later Yousef says:

items.ar: إحنا فخورين فيها كتير بنجاحها بالتوجيهي السنة الماضية.
items.translit: iḥna fakhūrīn fīha ktīr bi-najāḥha bit-tawjīhī is-sane il-māḍye.
items.en: We’re really proud of her for passing the Tawjihi exam last year.

paragraphs: You have already been working with verbal nouns in this chapter, and نجاح is another one. It means “success”, so نجاحها is literally “her success.” We are able to talk about her passing the exam without needing to introduce a new verb.
After all of that, Walid starts giving Yousef a little perspective, and Yousef responds with a phrase you are going to hear constantly:
This is one of those short expressions that shows up everywhere in conversation.
حَقّ has the idea of “right” or “truth,” so مَعَك حَقّ literally carries the sense of “the right is with you.” In natural English, though, it is simply:
You’re right.
In the dialogue, Yousef says:

items.ar: مَعَك حَقّ، بَسّ ما عِندها وَقْت لَحالها.
items.translit: maʿak ḥaʾʾ, bass mā ʿindha waʾt laḥālha.
items.en: You’re right, but she doesn’t have any time for herself

paragraphs: Another expression that comes up toward the end is:

items.en: What do you think of…? / How about…?

paragraphs: Walid says:

items.ar: شو رأيك بلمة عيلة بعد الامتحانات؟
items.translit: shū raʾyak bi-lammet ʿēle baʿd il-imtiḥānāt?
items.en: How about a family get-together after the exams?

paragraphs: You can think of شو رأيك بـ…؟ as literally asking, “What’s your opinion of…?” The بـ introduces whatever you are asking the person’s opinion about.
And that gives us another useful phrase:

A لمة is a gathering—people coming together in one place. You will hear it used a lot with family and friends, especially when people are talking about holidays, dinners, visits, or everybody getting together.
Yousef also mentions:

items.en: at the end of the year

paragraphs: We are going to get much deeper into expressions for parts of the day, week, month, and year later. For now, just notice بآخر… as a very useful way to talk about something happening “at the end of…”
Walid eventually suggests:

items.en: a little rest and a change of scenery

paragraphs: تغيير جو is a really common expression. Literally, it is something like “changing the atmosphere.” In real conversation, it is the idea of getting out, doing something different, taking a break, or changing your surroundings for a while.
And once again, something familiar is hiding inside the expression: تغيير is a verbal noun.
Toward the end Walid tells Yousef:

items.en: Patience is the key to relief.

paragraphs: This is a common saying, and it fits the situation pretty well. Everyone in Yousef’s family seems to have something going on—work, school, studying, exams, university—and Walid is basically reminding him that things will work themselves out.

That one works almost exactly like English. Literally, العشا is “the dinner” and عليّ is “on me.”

The important thing here is that you did not suddenly jump into a completely different level of Arabic. Most of this conversation was built out of things you already know. What is changing now is that those pieces are starting to sound more like an actual conversation.
